title: How Altonia Reads
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Reading habits are changing across the world, and the imaginary country of Altonia offers a useful example. Every five years since 1990, its national statistics office has asked thousands of adults how they read, what they read and where they get their books. The results, taken together, show four quite different patterns, and each has a story behind it. This passage describes the main findings and the explanations that researchers have offered, and it asks what they may mean for the future of reading in the country. The study is unusual because the same questions have been asked in the same way for more than thirty years, so that the answers can be compared directly. Its authors stress that the figures describe adults only, and that children may behave quite differently from their parents.

The most dramatic change concerns electronic books. For almost two decades, hardly anyone in Altonia read them: the figure stayed close to zero because readers were expensive and the choice of titles was small. Then, in the early 2010s, cheap tablets and larger phone screens arrived, and the number jumped within a few years. Today, more than a third of adults say that they read at least one e-book each year, and the share is still climbing, although more slowly than before.

Printed newspapers tell a very different story. In 1990, nearly three-quarters of adults read one at least once a week. The figure has fallen at every survey since, and it is now below one in five. Readers say they prefer to find news online, where it is free and constantly updated. Several famous titles have closed, and others now publish only a few days a week, relying on their websites for most of their income.

Library visits followed a pattern with a peak. Numbers rose during the 1990s, when many new libraries opened and the government ran a campaign to encourage reading among children. They reached their highest point in 2005. After that they fell sharply, partly because many libraries cut their opening hours when budgets were reduced, and partly because people could now borrow e-books from home. Some libraries have since changed, offering computer classes, meeting rooms and cafes, and the decline seems to have slowed.

Audiobooks developed in yet another way. They began as a small market for blind readers and for long car journeys, and for years the audience was tiny. A rapid rise followed the arrival of music-streaming services, which taught people to listen on their phones, but the growth has now stopped. About one adult in ten listens to an audiobook each year, and the figure has stayed at that level for the last decade, which suggests that the market has found its natural size. Publishers say that the loyal audience for audiobooks is mostly made up of commuters and of people over fifty who find it hard to read small print.

What does all this mean for the reading of books in general? Surprisingly, the total time that adults spend reading has hardly changed. The researcher in charge of the survey, Dr Sven Ahlberg, says that people have not stopped reading; they have changed the way they do it. He adds that readers who use several formats tend to read more books than those who use only one, so that digital reading may actually help to keep the habit alive.

Looking to the future, the survey team expects the same pattern to continue: more reading on screens, fewer printed newspapers, and a gradual change in the role of the library. Publishers, meanwhile, are experimenting with new ways to sell stories, from monthly subscriptions to books that are published one chapter at a time. Whether these experiments succeed will depend on whether readers are willing to pay for what they can often find free elsewhere, a question that nobody can yet answer with confidence.
